name: Thermage / monopolar RF

lead: Thermage is a clinic treatment people use to firm up mildly to moderately loose skin on the face, neck and eyelids and to soften fine lines, without surgery.

Monopolar radiofrequency heats the dermis while the surface is cooled, and the heat is said to stimulate collagen and elastin and remodel tissue. Early studies from 2003 to 2004 reported improvement in eye-area and cheek or neck laxity after single treatments. Published studies are mostly small device studies, many company-linked.

paras: It is delivered in a clinic by a trained practitioner, typically as a single session on the chosen area. The device was first sold as ThermaCool and is now marketed as Thermage FLX. Results build gradually as collagen remodels.
Pain, sometimes requiring sedation, and skin dents have been reported. Rare events include fat loss and scarring. Treatment is delivered by trained clinicians.

angle.text: Thermage is used in clinics to tighten mild-to-moderate skin laxity on the face, neck and eyelids so skin looks firmer and fine lines look softer. Radiofrequency heats the dermis, collagen tightens and remodels, and results show gradually. Small device studies have reported improvements in laxity scores.

lead: Thermage is a brand of non-ablative monopolar radiofrequency (RF) treatment used in clinics to tighten skin on the face, neck and eyelids, with body applications also offered. A handpiece delivers RF energy into the dermis while the surface is cooled, with the aim of firming lax skin and softening fine lines without incisions or downtime of the kind that follows surgery or ablative resurfacing.[1][2][3] The system was first sold as ThermaCool and is now marketed by Solta Medical, part of Bausch Health, as Thermage FLX.[4][3][5]

For appearance, the appeal is a firmer, smoother look where skin has loosened: the jawline, cheeks, neck, brow and the skin around the eyes, and, in the manufacturer's description, areas such as the abdomen and thighs after ageing, pregnancy or weight change.[3] RF skin tightening in general is described as heating the dermis to stimulate collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production, with a dermal target temperature of about 67 degrees C cited.[1][6] The treatment is usually positioned as an alternative to, or a step before, surgical lifting.[6]

Research consists mainly of device studies from 2003 onward. These include a multicentre periorbital study of 86 people, single-centre cheek and neck studies, a randomised comparison of one versus two treatments, a review of more than 600 treatments, and newer registered trials of Thermage FLX handpieces.[2][7][8][9][10][11] A 2007 plastic-surgery review described the published evidence as supporting use for mild to moderate facial skin laxity and wrinkles.[12] Reported effects include pain during treatment, temporary redness and swelling, and, rarely, burns, fat loss or scarring.[1][9][3]
infobox: Thermage, Inc. (Hayward, California), later Solta Medical; acquired by Valeant (now Bausch Health) in January 2014[2][5]
Face, neck, eyelids; body applications also studied[1][21][3]
30 to 60 minutes for a treatment area (manufacturer)[3]

paras: Radiofrequency skin tightening is a family of techniques that use RF energy to heat skin. Devices differ in how many electrodes they use, and penetration depth depends on the configuration, with monopolar, bipolar, unipolar and tripolar designs described.[1][6] Thermage is the best-known monopolar system. A 2007 review described its technology as nonablative monopolar capacitive RF that protects the skin surface while selectively heating the layer beneath, and noted that keeping the epidermis intact is what limits recovery time and complication risk compared with ablative resurfacing.[12]

Other manufacturers offer devices in the wider RF category, including bipolar and tripolar systems and microneedle RF, which Wikipedia describes as the newest form of delivery.[1][6] Hair-related RF is a separate topic: a 2023 review found most RF hair studies concerned hair removal, with some reports of growth depending on modality.[13]

The manufacturer describes a handpiece that delivers RF energy while providing cooling and vibration for comfort, with energy delivery adjusting during the procedure, and says the device is meant to support the body's own collagen remodelling.[3] Treatment categories it lists are the full face, targeted zones such as cheeks, jawline, mouth area or forehead, the eyelids and skin around the eyes, and the body, including abdomen, thighs, above the knees and under the bra line.[3]

RF energy heats the dermis, and the heating is said to stimulate collagen production and remodelling.[1] By adjusting how the skin is cooled, RF can also be used to heat deeper tissue or fat.[1] A cited dermal target temperature for inducing remodelling and reducing wrinkles and laxity is 67 degrees C, and delivering power until that temperature is reached is described as optimising results.[1][6]

Two phases of result are described. The manufacturer says some people see immediate tightening and that visible improvement continues over about two to six months as collagen remodels.[3] The 2004 randomised comparison found that both one-treatment and two-treatment groups kept improving between the one-month and four-month assessments.[8] In a 2006 forum post about loose skin after fat loss, one T Nation user wrote that changes take around four months to appear and that they felt it was helping at two months.[14]

A 2005 split-scar study of ThermaCool treatment in hypertrophic and keloid scars found collagen production rising, with type III exceeding type I and peaking about six to ten weeks after treatment, which the authors saw as relevant to the device's effects on dermal collagen.[15]

Treatment takes place in a clinic. The manufacturer says most sessions run 30 to 60 minutes depending on the area, that a single treatment delivers results so multiple sessions are not required, that results can last one to two years, and that annual maintenance treatments are suggested to keep the effect.[3] Published studies have used single sessions followed for up to six months, and one randomised comparison tested a second session a month later.[2][7][8]

Pain during treatment is the most-discussed experience, and studies have examined it. A 2005 trial of 84 women compared RF tightening with and without topical anaesthesia and found that anaesthesia reduced pain without significantly raising the energy level people could tolerate and did not affect the final efficacy.[16] Wikipedia notes reports of pain needing sedation in some patients and that vacuum applied at the treatment point has reportedly reduced burning and crusting.[1]

The manufacturer says the device should not be used in people with pacemakers or other implanted electrical devices, and lists conditions and situations for which it has not studied the device, including pregnancy, breastfeeding, diabetes, autoimmune disease and permanent makeup or tattoos.[3] A 2006 pilot study examined RF applied two weeks after hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite filler injections in six subjects and saw no gross changes in the filler or surrounding skin on biopsy, with slightly more transient pain over filler; the authors called for further study.[17]

The ThermaCool system was developed by Thermage, Inc. of Hayward, California.[2] The manufacturer dates its use to 2002 and says more than five million treatments have been performed worldwide, a figure it bases on treatment tips sold; a 2006 review stated that monopolar RF skin tightening had been used on over 10,000 patients since 2002, and its retrospective series began in May 2002.[9][3]

Early published studies appeared in 2003 and 2004 and covered the periorbital area, cheeks, neck and lower face.[2][7][8][18] The system was marketed in that period as a non-surgical facelift, a phrase used in a 2003 clinical trial title.[18] Wikipedia records that Valeant, now Bausch Health, acquired Solta Medical in January 2014 for about 250 million dollars, and that Thermage FLX received Health Canada clearance in April 2025.[5] The brand's current handpieces are listed for the face, neck and eyelids, with body treatment categories on the manufacturer's site.[4][3]

The 2003 multicentre ThermaCool study enrolled 86 subjects who each received one periorbital treatment. Blinded photo scoring found Fitzpatrick wrinkle-score improvement of at least one point in 83.2 percent of 119 treated periorbital areas at six months, treating physicians without pre-treatment photographs judged 28.9 percent of 166 areas improved, and 50 percent of subjects said they were satisfied or very satisfied. Objective photo analysis found 61.5 percent of eyebrows lifted by at least 0.5 mm.[2]

A 2004 study of 50 patients (30 with cheek laxity and 20 with neck laxity) used one session after topical anaesthetic and masked assessors graded photographs up to six months. Most patients showed significant improvement, tightening was still visible at six months, and the authors noted that durability beyond six months was unknown.[7]

A 2004 randomised comparison of 20 patients with mild to moderate laxity of the middle and lower face gave one treatment to 11 and two treatments a month apart to nine. Four blinded physicians rated photographs at one and four months; the two-treatment group scored higher in every category, with the nasolabial-fold difference significant, and patients who had two treatments reported more improvement at four months. The authors described the overall improvement as modest and satisfaction as relatively high, and noted the small sample.[8] A 2003 trial treated 20 areas in 17 patients around the brow and jowls and reported gradual tightening in most patients with no adverse effects.[18]

The 2007 review concluded that published evidence supports use for mild to moderate laxity and wrinkles and called monopolar capacitive RF the current gold standard for noninvasive skin tightening.[12] More recently, a randomised trial of 42 women published in 2025 found that adding topical repair and anti-ageing products to a single Thermage treatment produced greater improvement in hydration, elasticity, density, fine lines, texture and pores at four weeks than the procedure alone.[19]

A retrospective review of more than 600 consecutive treatments from May 2002 to June 2006 found temporary side effects in 2.7 percent of treatments and no permanent side effects. Redness and swelling were the usual expected effects, usually lasting under 24 hours; six patients had swelling for up to a week; one cheek depression resolved within about three and a half months; and neck tenderness lasted two to three weeks in a few patients. The authors concluded the procedure was very safe with infrequent, self-limited, minor side effects.[9]

In the 2003 multicentre periorbital study, second-degree burns occurred in 0.36 percent of 5,858 RF applications and three patients had small areas of residual scarring at six months.[2] Wikipedia reports that improper technique can cause skin dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported, though newer techniques reportedly address this.[1]

The manufacturer lists pain during treatment, redness usually fading within 24 hours and swelling usually fading within five days as common effects, and burns, blisters, scarring, skin irregularities, numbness or tingling (rarely temporary paralysis), lumps or nodules mostly in the neck, and temporary skin darkening as less common ones.[3] Treatment is delivered by trained clinicians using the manufacturer's handpieces.

Monopolar RF has been examined outside the face. A report on 37 Asian patients combined Thermage with a 585-nm pulsed dye laser for abdominal stretch marks; 89.2 percent rated the result good or very good, and biopsies in nine patients showed more collagen fibres, with more elastic fibres in six, though the authors noted pigmentary risk in darker skin.[20] A 2009 report on 12 subjects used a multiplex tip for body shaping and found average waist circumference and skin-laxity scores falling through six months of follow-up.[21]

In the 2005 scar study of ten people with hypertrophic or keloid scars, treated and untreated thirds of each scar did not differ clinically or histologically at 24 weeks, though collagen effects were seen and the authors called for further study.[15] Newer registered studies cover a non-Thermage monopolar RF device for facial wrinkles (n=284) and a comparison of Ulthera ultrasound and Thermage for the face and neck (n=20).[22][23]

Thermage appears in bodybuilding and fitness forums mostly as a non-surgical option for loose skin after weight loss or pregnancy. In a 2008 T Nation thread on loose skin after children, a poster listed Thermage among non-surgical tightening options and said they did not know how effective they were.[24] In a 2014 thread a poster mentioned RF devices of the kind used on the face to shrink or tighten loose skin, saying clinics use different names for them and that they believed Thermage was one.[25] In 2006, a user described trying several measures, including Thermage, for love handles at low body fat.[14]

Published studies include multicentre and single-centre device studies in the periorbital area, cheek and neck, and middle and lower face, a randomised one-versus-two-treatment comparison, and a large retrospective safety review.[2][7][8][9] The 2007 review judged the published evidence to support use for mild to moderate laxity.[12]

Registered trials include Thermage FLX on face, neck and eyelids (n=25, started 2019), a lower-face and submentum study (n=12), a 50-person study of the CPT handpiece for facial and neck laxity, a feasibility comparison of Ulthera versus Thermage for face and neck (n=20), a monopolar RF facial wrinkle study (n=284), and a controlled safety and effectiveness study of Thermage FLX (n=164) registered in 2025.[4][10][11][22][23][26]

Other non-surgical approaches discussed alongside RF for skin laxity include microneedle RF, focused ultrasound (the Ulthera comparison above), fractional laser resurfacing, and surgical lifting, which RF is positioned as an alternative to.[1][22][6] Other devices in the RF family include Venus Legacy, VelaShape and Exilis for body contouring, listed in Wikipedia.[1][6]

lore.intro: Thermage is mentioned in fitness and bodybuilding forums mainly as a clinic option for loose skin and is not a major topic of community protocol discussion; most claims come from clinic and manufacturer descriptions rather than forum posters.[14][24][3][25]

claims.claim: Thermage can tighten loose skin after weight loss without surgery
It is a non-surgical alternative to a facelift
One treatment is enough and results last one to two years
The results keep improving for months afterwards
Pain limits how much energy can be delivered, so numbing cream improves results
Combining it with skincare products improves outcomes
It can treat scars and stretch marks

timeline.event: Monopolar RF skin tightening enters clinical use; the manufacturer dates the brand to 2002 and the 2006 retrospective series begins in May 2002.[9][3]
Multicentre periorbital tightening study of 86 subjects and a non-surgical RF facelift trial published.[2][18]
Studies of cheek and neck laxity (50 patients) and of one versus two treatments (20 patients) published.[7][8]
Studies of RF with and without topical anaesthesia and of scars and keloids published.[16][15]
Retrospective analysis of over 600 treatments published; use reported on over 10,000 patients.[9]
Review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics describes evidence supporting use for mild to moderate laxity.[12]
Body-shaping report on 12 subjects with a multiplex tip.[21]
Valeant acquires Solta Medical, Thermage's maker, for about 250 million dollars.[5]
Registered study of Thermage FLX on face, neck and eyelids begins.[10]
Randomised trial of adding topical cosmetics to Thermage published; Thermage FLX receives Health Canada clearance in April; controlled FLX study (n=164) registered.[11][19][5]
